claim: Runs-of-homozygosity (ROH) segments are contiguous homozygous regions in a genome traditionally linked to families and inbred populations.
source: Runs-of-homozygosity (ROH) segments, contiguous homozygous regions in a genome were traditionally linked to families and inbred populations.
evidence: This is a statement about the traditional understanding of ROH, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A growing literature suggests that ROHs are ubiquitous in outbred populations.
source: However, a growing literature suggests that ROHs are ubiquitous in outbred populations.
evidence: This claim references existing literature on the topic, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Most existing genetic studies of ROH in populations are limited to aggregated ROH content across the genome.
source: Still, most existing genetic studies of ROH in populations are limited to aggregated ROH content across the genome, which does not offer the resolution for mapping causal loci.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing studies based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Aggregated ROH content analysis does not offer the resolution for mapping causal loci.
source: Still, most existing genetic studies of ROH in populations are limited to aggregated ROH content across the genome, which does not offer the resolution for mapping causal loci.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of aggregated analysis methods.

claim: The limitation of ROH studies is mainly due to a lack of methods for the efficient identification of shared ROH diplotypes.
source: This limitation is mainly due to a lack of methods for the efficient identification of shared ROH diplotypes.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of limitations in the field.

claim: ROH-DICE identified over 1 million ROH diplotypes that span over 100 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and are shared by more than 100 UK Biobank participants.
source: ROH-DICE identified over 1 million ROH diplotypes that span over 100 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and are shared by more than 100 UK Biobank participants.
evidence: This is a direct report of data obtained from applying the ROH-DICE method to UK Biobank data.

claim: Significant associations of clustered ROH diplotypes across the genome with various self-reported diseases were found.
source: Moreover, we found significant associations of clustered ROH diplotypes across the genome with various self-reported diseases, with the strongest associations found between the extended human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region and autoimmune disorders.
evidence: This is a finding from the association analysis performed in the study.

claim: The strongest associations were found between the extended human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region and autoimmune disorders.
source: Moreover, we found significant associations of clustered ROH diplotypes across the genome with various self-reported diseases, with the strongest associations found between the extended human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region and autoimmune disorders.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the association analysis.

claim: An association was found between a diplotype covering the homeostatic iron regulator (HFE) gene and hemochromatosis.
source: We found an association between a diplotype covering the homeostatic iron regulator (HFE) gene and hemochromatosis, even though the well-known causal SNP was not directly genotyped or imputed.
evidence: This is a specific association finding from the study.

claim: The well-known causal SNP for hemochromatosis was not directly genotyped or imputed in the UK Biobank data.
source: We found an association between a diplotype covering the homeostatic iron regulator (HFE) gene and hemochromatosis, even though the well-known causal SNP was not directly genotyped or imputed.
evidence: This is a statement about the data availability in UK Biobank.

claim: A putative association was identified between carriers of an ROH diplotype in chromosome 4 and an increase in mortality among COVID-19 patients (p-value = 1.82 × 10−11).
source: Using a genome-wide scan, we identified a putative association between carriers of an ROH diplotype in chromosome 4 and an increase in mortality among COVID-19 patients (p-value = 1.82 × 10−11).
evidence: This is a specific association finding with statistical support from the study.

claim: ROH regions are regions of diploid chromosomes where identical-by-descent (IBD) haplotypes are inherited from each parent.
source: Runs-of-homozygosity (ROH) regions are regions of diploid chromosomes where identical-by-descent (IBD) haplotypes are inherited from each parent (Ceballos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: ROH may be linked to consanguinity and population isolation.
source: Traditionally, ROH was thought to be relevant only to inbred populations, and ROH may be linked to consanguinity and population isolation (Kirin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A growing number of studies of large cohorts and biobanks have found that ROH may be ubiquitously present.
source: However, a growing number of studies of large cohorts and biobanks have found that ROH may be ubiquitously present (Clark et al., 2019; Joshi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has long been known that inbreeding is harmful to the health of offspring.
source: It has long been known that inbreeding is harmful to the health of offspring (Morton et al., 1956), and several studies have suggested that the global ROH content is associated with higher risks of recessive disorders (Lencz et al., 2007; Keller et al., 2012; Christofidou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established knowledge.

claim: Several studies have suggested that the global ROH content is associated with higher risks of recessive disorders.
source: It has long been known that inbreeding is harmful to the health of offspring (Morton et al., 1956), and several studies have suggested that the global ROH content is associated with higher risks of recessive disorders (Lencz et al., 2007; Keller et al., 2012; Christofidou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ROHs can be related to complex traits such as height.
source: ROHs can also be related to complex traits such as height (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: People with extremely long ROH can be found even in outbred populations.
source: A recent study (Yengo et al., 2019) revealed that people with extremely long ROH can be found even in outbred populations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Homozygosity mapping in pedigree or inbred populations has achieved success in identifying recessive loci.
source: Indeed, homozygosity mapping in pedigree or inbred populations has achieved success in identifying recessive loci (Keller et al., 2012; Lander and Botstein, 1987; Leutenegger et al., 2006; Pourreza et al., 2020; Tischfield et al., 2005; Gandin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous successful studies.

claim: For general outbred populations, the total number of possible ROH diplotypes at a locus is too enormous to be enumerated efficiently.
source: However, for general outbred populations, the total number of possible ROH diplotypes at a locus is too enormous to be enumerated efficiently, and ROH mapping of outbred populations has remained only a theoretical possibility.
evidence: This is an inference about computational limitations in the field.

claim: ROH mapping of outbred populations has remained only a theoretical possibility.
source: However, for general outbred populations, the total number of possible ROH diplotypes at a locus is too enormous to be enumerated efficiently, and ROH mapping of outbred populations has remained only a theoretical possibility.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field before this work.

claim: The chance of ROH is determined by the chance of a pair of mates having IBD.
source: Such ROH diplotypes are of interest because they are at the extreme of distribution: the chance of ROH is determined by the chance of a pair of mates having IBD, and such chance and also the length of IBD segments will decay quickly in outbred populations, as supported by population genetics theory (Thompson, 2013; Donnelly, 1983) and real-world data (Ralph and Coop, 2013; Naseri et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by population genetics theory and citations.

claim: The chance and length of IBD segments will decay quickly in outbred populations.
source: Such ROH diplotypes are of interest because they are at the extreme of distribution: the chance of ROH is determined by the chance of a pair of mates having IBD, and such chance and also the length of IBD segments will decay quickly in outbred populations, as supported by population genetics theory (Thompson, 2013; Donnelly, 1983) and real-world data (Ralph and Coop, 2013; Naseri et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by population genetics theory and real-world data with citations.

claim: Each cluster of ROH diplotypes is defined as a set of 100 consecutive homozygous sites that are shared among over 100 individuals.
source: Each cluster of ROH diplotypes is defined as a set of 100 consecutive homozygous sites that are shared among over 100 individuals.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: A total of 1,880,826 ROH clusters were identified in all 22 autosomal chromosomes.
source: A total of 1,880,826 ROH clusters (shared among at least 100 individuals and extending at least 100 consecutive sites) were identified in all 22 autosomal chromosomes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the analysis.

claim: The average length of ROH clusters is 553,095 bp (~0.55 cM).
source: The average length of these ROHs is 553,095 bp (~0.55 cM).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data.

claim: The number of ROH clusters in chromosome 6 is the highest.
source: Interestingly, the number of ROH clusters in chromosome 6 is the highest.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The high number of ROH clusters in chromosome 6 is mainly due to the excessive number of ROH clusters in the MHC region (65,458).
source: This is mainly due to the excessive number of ROH clusters in the MHC region (65,458).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing concentration in the MHC region.

claim: A peak region in chromosome 2 (chr2:135755899–136827560) has been reported to harbor a high selection signal.
source: A peak region in chromosome 2 (chr2:135755899–136827560) has been reported to harbor a high selection signal (Browning and Browning, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The chromosome 2 peak region contains the lactase gene (LCT) gene which includes a variant selected for lactose tolerance in the European population.
source: This region contains the lactase gene (LCT) gene which includes a variant selected for lactose tolerance in the European population (Itan et al., 2009), though the current understanding of the selection pressure is more nuanced (Mathieson and Terhorst, 2022; Evershed et al., 2022; Le et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The peak in chromosome 8 (chr8:42531565–42629520) contains two known genes, CHRNB3 and CHRNA6.
source: The peak in chromosome 8 (chr8:42531565–42629520) contains two known genes, CHRNB3 and CHRNA6.
evidence: This is a statement about gene content in a genomic region.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the significant role of the CHRNB3–CHRNA6 gene cluster on chromosome 8 in nicotine dependence.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated the significant role of the CHRNB3–CHRNA6 gene cluster on chromosome 8 in nicotine dependence (Wen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An earlier study has identified strong evidence for selection in the CHRNB3–CHRNA6 region.
source: Additionally, an earlier study has identified strong evidence for selection in the CHRNB3–CHRNA6 region (Sadler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some clusters comprise more than a hundred thousand individuals sharing the same ROH consensus.
source: Surprisingly, some clusters comprise more than a hundred thousand individuals sharing the same ROH consensus.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The high rate of ROH clusters in the MHC region may be attributed to the high density of markers and low recombination rates.
source: The high rate of ROH clusters in the MHC region may be attributed to the high density of markers and low recombination rates (Traherne, 2008; Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The correlation coefficient between combined ROH classes in the European population and the ROH clusters in UKBB was 0.54.
source: The correlation coefficient between combined ROH classes in the European population (Pemberton et al., 2012) and the ROH clusters in UKBB was 0.54.
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing datasets.

claim: 61 associations passed the Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold of 10−12.
source: This identified 61 associations passing the Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold of 10−12.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis.

claim: The most prominent associations found are ROH diplotypes in the HLA region with autoimmune diseases.
source: Not surprisingly, the most prominent associations we found are ROH diplotypes in the HLA region with autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the association analysis.

claim: Malabsorption/coeliac disease, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis have the strongest association with loci in the HLA region.
source: We found that malabsorption/coeliac disease, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis have the strongest association with loci in the HLA region.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the association analysis.

claim: These results are largely consistent with known literature.
source: These results are largely consistent with known literature (Dieli-Crimi et al., 2015; Gutierrez-Achury et al., 2015; Kurkó et al., 2013; Bhalerao and Bowcock, 1998; Baranzini and Oksenberg, 2017; Canela-Xandri et al., 2018).

claim: One of the most significant associations identified is the association between the ROH diplotype at chr6:25988167–26122453 and hemochromatosis (p-value = 9.16 × 10−120).
source: One of the most significant associations we identified is the association between the ROH diplotype at chr6:25988167–26122453 and hemochromatosis (p-value = 9.16 × 10−120).
evidence: This is a specific association finding with statistical support.

claim: The frequency of the ROH diplotype associated with hemochromatosis is only 0.02%.
source: The frequency of the ROH diplotype is only 0.02% and the odds ratio of having the disease for the carrier is 102.21.
evidence: This is a statistical description of the data.

claim: The odds ratio of having hemochromatosis for the carrier of the ROH diplotype is 102.21.
source: The frequency of the ROH diplotype is only 0.02% and the odds ratio of having the disease for the carrier is 102.21.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the association analysis.

claim: Hemochromatosis is an inherited disorder in which iron levels in the body slowly build up over several years.
source: Hemochromatosis is an inherited disorder in which iron levels in the body slowly build up over several years.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the disease.

claim: The gene HFE (chr6:26087509–26095469) is a well-known recessive locus for hemochromatosis.
source: The gene HFE (chr6:26087509–26095469) is a well-known recessive locus for this disease (Pietrangelo, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The C282Y polymorphism (rs1800562, chr6:26092913) in HFE is the most penetrant.
source: The C282Y polymorphism (rs1800562, chr6:26092913) in HFE is the most penetrant but other polymorphisms with lesser penetrance are also known.

claim: The minor allele frequency of the SNP rs1800562 is 6% in the European population.
source: Interestingly, the minor allele frequency of the SNP rs1800562 is 6% in the European population but it is not genotyped (and is also not available in the imputed panel) in the UK Biobank data.
evidence: This is a statement about allele frequency in a population.

claim: The SNP rs1800562 is not genotyped and is also not available in the imputed panel in the UK Biobank data.
source: Interestingly, the minor allele frequency of the SNP rs1800562 is 6% in the European population but it is not genotyped (and is also not available in the imputed panel) in the UK Biobank data.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability in UK Biobank.

claim: The hemochromatosis association signal has been completely missing in the Neale Lab results.
source: As a result, this association signal has been completely missing in the Neale Lab results.
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of a signal in another analysis.

claim: In another study, the SNP rs1800562 has been imputed and a specific association study for the recessive effect between the homozygous alleles of rs1800562 and hemochromatosis has been reported.
source: In another study, the SNP has been imputed and a specific association study for the recessive effect between the homozygous alleles of rs1800562 and hemochromatosis has been reported (Tamosauskaite et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to another study.

claim: The most prominent ROH diplotype association outside of the HLA region is at chr1:151515188–151902494 with eczema/dermatitis.
source: The most prominent one is an ROH diplotype at chr1:151515188–151902494 with eczema/dermatitis.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the association analysis.

claim: The eczema/dermatitis signal overlaps with the GWAS finding of rs4845604 at chr1:151829204.
source: This signal overlaps with the GWAS finding of rs4845604 at chr1:151829204 (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous GWAS results supported by a citation.

claim: The most significant ROH region associated with COVID-19 mortality is located in chr4:106318456–106483898 (0.114 cM) with the p-value 1.63 × 10−10.
source: The most significant ROH region is located in chr4:106318456–106483898 (0.114 cM) with the p-value 1.63 × 10−10.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the COVID-19 mortality association analysis.

claim: 4389 individuals share the diplotypes associated with COVID-19 mortality and 76 of them have tested positive for COVID-19.
source: 4389 individuals share the diplotypes and 76 of them have tested positive for COVID-19.
evidence: This is a description of the data for the COVID-19 association.

claim: Eleven persons who carried the same ROH consensus and had tested positive for COVID-19, died in 2020.
source: Eleven persons who carried the same ROH consensus and had tested positive, died in 2020.
evidence: This is a description of the data for the COVID-19 mortality association.

claim: Carriers of the chr4 diplotype have a fivefold mortality compared to non-carriers among COVID-19 patients.
source: In other words, carriers of this diplotype have a fivefold mortality compared to non-carriers among COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a statistical inference from the data.

claim: The reported p-value from GMMAT mixed model regression for the chr4 diplotype and COVID-19 mortality was 1.82 × 10−11.
source: We used the GMMAT (Hoare, 1961) mixed model regression to validate the association of this diplotype while adjusting for age, gender, and genetic similarity (see Methods section). The reported p-value was 1.82 × 10−11 which is even smaller than the p-value from the chi-square test.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical validation analysis.

claim: The region associated with COVID-19 mortality includes the PPA2 gene.
source: The region includes the PPA2 gene.
evidence: This is a statement about gene content in the genomic region.

claim: The PPA2 gene product is an inorganic pyrophosphatase located in the mitochondrion.
source: The gene product is an inorganic pyrophosphatase located in the mitochondrion (Curbo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gene supported by a citation.

claim: Missense mutations in the PPA2 gene are reported to cause sudden unexpected cardiac arrest in infancy.
source: Missense mutations in this gene are reported to cause sudden unexpected cardiac arrest in infancy (Guimier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The PPA2 gene has been recently implicated in COVID-19 through an integrated analysis of GWAS of European patients and lung expressed quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data by the summary-data-based (SMR) method.
source: The PPA2 gene has also been recently implicated in COVID-19 through an integrated analysis of GWAS of European patients and lung expressed quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data by the summary-data-based (SMR) method (Zong and Li, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: The identified region linked to COVID-19 mortality overlaps with the ARHGEF38 gene.
source: The identified region linked to COVID-19 mortality overlaps also with the ARHGEF38 gene.
evidence: This is a statement about gene content in the genomic region.

claim: A genetic variant within the ARHGEF38 gene (rs72670002) has been reported to be significantly associated with severe illness from COVID-19 in a recent study that used 24,202 cases of critical COVID-19.
source: A genetic variant within the gene (rs72670002) has been reported to be significantly associated with severe illness from COVID-19 in a recent study that used 24,202 cases of critical COVID-19 (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Other nearby genes within a 200-kb range of the COVID-19 mortality-associated region include TET2, INTS12, and GSTCD.
source: Other nearby genes within a 200-kb range include TET2, INTS12, and GSTCD.
evidence: This is a statement about gene content in the genomic region.

claim: The running time of the ROH-DICE algorithm is linear to the size of the genotype panel.
source: The running time of the algorithm is linear to the size of the genotype panel which enables fast processing of millions of individuals without requiring extravagant resources.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational complexity of the algorithm.

claim: ROH-DICE enables fast processing of millions of individuals without requiring extravagant resources.
source: The running time of the algorithm is linear to the size of the genotype panel which enables fast processing of millions of individuals without requiring extravagant resources.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of the algorithm's efficiency.

claim: Large ROH clusters can be used to identify signatures of selection in humans or other species.
source: Large ROH clusters can be used to identify signatures of selection in humans or other species.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications of the method.

claim: Positive selection reduces haplotype diversity, increasing homozygosity around the target locus, resulting in higher frequencies of ROH in regions containing selection loci.
source: Positive selection reduces haplotype diversity, increasing homozygosity around the target locus, resulting in higher frequencies of ROH in regions containing selection loci (Pemberton et al., 2012; Sabeti et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about selection supported by citations.

claim: Excessive ROH regions can be linked to selective sweeps and have been found to coincide with positive selection in humans and other species.
source: Therefore, excessive ROH regions can be linked to selective sweeps and have been found to coincide with positive selection in humans (Pemberton et al., 2012), and other species (Hewett et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Three large ROH clusters in chromosomes 2, 6, and 8 of UKBB overlap with known hotspots for selection signals.
source: Three large ROH clusters in chromosomes 2, 6, and 8 of UKBB overlap with known hotspots for selection signals.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the data with known selection hotspots.

claim: The existing GWAS are mainly testing the additive effects of single SNPs, while ROH-DICE is testing the recessive effects of relatively long haplotypes.
source: The existing GWAS are mainly testing the additive effects of single SNPs, while we are testing the recessive effects of relatively long haplotypes.
evidence: This is a comparison of the genetic effects being tested by different methods.

claim: The ROH-DICE analysis is similar to traditional family-based homozygosity mapping, but at a population scale.
source: In a sense, our analysis is similar to traditional family-based homozygosity mapping (Lander and Botstein, 1987), but at a population scale.
evidence: This is a comparison with traditional methods supported by a citation.

claim: ROH-DICE is not meant to replace regular GWAS, but to complement it.
source: It is important to note that ROH-DICE is not meant to replace regular GWAS, but to complement it.
evidence: This is a statement about the intended use of the method.

claim: When the causal variant is located in a long ROH diplotype shared by many individuals (ROH diplotype clusters), ROH-DICE outperforms regular GWAS.
source: Specifically, when the causal variant is located in a long ROH diplotype shared by many individuals (ROH diplotype clusters), ROH-DICE outperforms regular GWAS.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation study.

claim: Genetic principal components can reduce the confounding effect brought on by population structure but it may be insufficient to completely eliminate the effects of recent demographic structure and the local environment.
source: Genetic principal components can reduce the confounding effect brought on by population structure but it may be insufficient to completely eliminate the effects of recent demographic structure and the local environment (Zaidi and Mathieson, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the method supported by a citation.

claim: Individuals sharing excessive ROH diplotypes may share similar environments since they are closely related and reside close to one another.
source: For example, individuals sharing excessive ROH diplotypes may share similar environments since they are closely related and reside close to one another.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential confounding factors.

source: Since we did not rule out related individuals, some of the reported GWAS signals may not be attributable to ROH.

source: The time complexity of this algorithm is O(NM), where N denotes the number of variant sites and M denotes the number of individuals.

source: This was achieved by running the ROH-DICE program, with a wall clock time of 18 hr and 54 min where the program was executed for all chromosomes in parallel (total CPU hours of ~242.5 hr).
evidence: This is a report of the computational performance of the method.

claim: The maximum residence size for each chromosome was approximately 180 MB.
source: The maximum residence size for each chromosome was approximately 180 MB.

source: 56,972 people with self-reported non-British ethnicity in UK Biobank were filtered out.

claim: For a pair of 100 sites genotype sequences, there is a very small probability that they will be mapped to the same compressed haplotype.
source: On average ~18% of sites are heterozygous, and thus for a pair of 100 sites genotype sequences, there is a very small probability that they will be mapped to the same compressed haplotype.

claim: The rate of false positives should be low.
source: Thus, the rate of false positives should be low.
